title: Space robots and rovers
keyIdea: A rover is a robot on wheels that explores another world for us. No person has been to Mars: it is very far away, very cold and has no air we can breathe, so robots go instead. Engineers on Earth talk to a Mars rover by radio, but each message takes about 3 to 22 minutes to get there, so they plan a whole drive and the rover follows the plan. Rovers such as Curiosity and Perseverance take photos, drill into rocks and test them, and have found rocks that show Mars had rivers and a lake long ago.
familyTip: Play 'Mars rover' at home: one person is the rover with eyes closed, the other writes a list of steps (2 steps forward, turn left, 3 steps forward) to reach a toy without bumping a chair, then hands over the whole list and stays silent while the rover follows it. Next, look at a real photo from Perseverance on NASA's Mars 2020 raw images page and spot rounded pebbles or layered rock together.

visual.caption: True about Mars, or not? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Its air is too thin for us to breathe
A rocket takes about 7 months to get there
A radio message gets there at once

lab.caption: Flagship lab: why robots go to Mars, time a radio message, plan a drive round craters, match tools, find rocks made by water, check a robot.

kid: A rover is a robot on wheels. It goes to places that are hard for people to reach. Rovers have driven on Mars and on the Moon.
No person has been to Mars yet. It is far away. The trip takes about 7 months. It is very cold, and the air is too thin to breathe. A rover does not breathe or eat, so it can go first.

We talk to a rover by radio. Radio is very fast, but Mars is so far that a message takes minutes to get there. So no one can steer it like a toy car. People plan the drive, and the rover does the plan.
A rover is like a lab on wheels. It has cameras, a drill and a laser to test rocks. Rovers found round pebbles and rocks made in a lake. They show that Mars had water long ago.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This builds on what astronauts do and leads on to the history of space exploration. Key words: rover, robot, Mars, engineer, radio signal, delay, route, crater, sample, drill, evidence.

Facts to know (NASA): Mars is about 55 to 400 million km from Earth, depending on where both planets are in their orbits. Radio travels at the speed of light, about 300,000 km each second, so a message takes about 3 to 22 minutes one way. A spacecraft takes about 7 months to get there. Mars averages about −60 °C, and its thin air is mostly carbon dioxide. Sojourner (1997) was the first Mars rover. Curiosity landed in Gale Crater in 2012 and found rounded stream pebbles and lake mudstone. Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater, an old lake, in 2021. It seals rock cores in tubes so they could be brought to Earth one day.

A common mistake is to think engineers drive a rover live with a joystick. The delay makes that impossible, so each day's drive is planned and sent, and the rover uses its own hazard cameras to stop or steer round danger. Children also often think Mars has rivers today, or that people are not allowed there. Mars is dry now; rocks show water long ago. People have not gone yet because of the distance, the cold and the lack of breathable air.

In the lab your child opens four Mars panels to see why robots go first, times a radio message with Mars near and far, plans a whole drive round craters before sending it, matches jobs to the rover's tools, picks the three rocks made by water, and checks a robot's sayings.

practice.prompt: A rover drives {a} metres on Monday and {b} metres on Tuesday. How far does it drive in the two days?
practice.explain: {a} m + {b} m = {=a+b} m. Rovers drive short distances each day because every drive is planned carefully.

practice.prompt: A radio message takes {a} minutes to reach Mars. The rover's reply takes {a} minutes to come back. How many minutes do the engineers wait in all?
practice.hint: The message goes there and the reply comes back: add {a} twice.
practice.explain: {a} + {a} = {=2*a} minutes. That wait is why engineers send a whole plan instead of steering live.

practice.prompt: Why do we send rovers to Mars instead of people?
choices: Mars is far, very cold and has no air we can breathe
People are not allowed to go to Mars
Mars is too small to stand on
practice.hint: Think about what a person needs to stay alive.
practice.explain: People need air, warmth and food for a 7-month trip. A rover needs none of these, so robots explore Mars first.

practice.prompt: Which rover tool can get powder from inside a rock?
choices: The drill on its arm
The mast cameras
The wheels
practice.hint: Which tool can make a hole?
practice.explain: The drill bores into the rock. The powder or core is then tested or kept in a sample tube.

practice.prompt: A rover finds round, smooth pebbles on Mars. What does this tell us?
choices: Water once flowed there and rolled them smooth
Wind piled them into a dune
A space rock just hit there
practice.hint: Think of pebbles in a stream or on a beach.
practice.explain: Flowing water rolls stones until their edges wear smooth. Curiosity found pebbles like this from an old stream bed.

pool.prompt: A rover drives {a} metres each day for {b} days. How far does it drive?
pool.hint: Add {a} metres once for each day, or multiply {a} by {b}.
pool.explain: {b} days of {a} m is {=a*b} m. Short drives keep the rover safe from craters and big rocks.

pool.prompt: A message to Mars takes {a} minutes one way. Engineers send it at 10:00. At how many minutes past 10 does it reach the rover?
pool.hint: The message leaves at 10:00 and travels for {a} minutes.
pool.explain: It arrives {a} minutes after 10:00, so at {a} minutes past 10. Anything the rover does in that time cannot be stopped.

pool.prompt: How do engineers get a rover round a crater?
choices: They plan the path and send the whole plan
They steer it live with a joystick
An astronaut on Mars pushes it
pool.hint: Each message takes minutes to reach Mars.
pool.explain: Live steering is impossible with a delay of minutes, and no people are on Mars. The rover follows a planned path.

pool.prompt: Is there a river flowing on Mars today?
choices: No, but rocks show it had water long ago
Yes, rovers have seen rivers flowing
No, and it never had any water
pool.hint: Think about round pebbles and lake mud layers.
pool.explain: Mars is a dry desert now. Rounded pebbles, mud layers and white veins show rivers and a lake long ago.

pool.prompt: What does Perseverance do with the rock cores it drills?
choices: Seals them in tubes so they could come to Earth one day
Flies them back to Earth the same day
Throws them away after a photo
pool.hint: The cores are kept safe for a later mission.
pool.explain: The cores are sealed in sample tubes. A future mission could carry them to Earth for scientists to study.

pool.prompt: Which rock is a clue that water was once on Mars?
choices: Rock with thin flat layers of mud
A sharp, broken rock
A dune of dust piled by wind
pool.hint: Mud settles slowly at the bottom of still water.
pool.explain: Flat mud layers form at the bottom of a lake. Sharp rock and dust dunes need no water.

pool.prompt: Which is true about a rover's speed?
choices: It drives slower than you walk
It drives as fast as a car on a road
It never moves, it only takes photos
pool.hint: Its top speed is about 150 metres in an hour.
pool.explain: About 150 m in an hour is much slower than walking. Driving slowly keeps the rover safe on rocky ground.

pool.prompt: Why does a rover not need food or air like an astronaut?
choices: It is a machine that runs on electricity
It eats Mars rocks
It brings a picnic from Earth
pool.hint: A robot is a machine, not a living thing.
pool.explain: A rover is a machine. It runs on electricity, so it needs no food, water or air.
